blocks.text: Śiva Sūtras 3.33
blocks.directed: [long pause] Śiva Sūtras 3.33

blocks.text: सुखदुःखयोर्बहिर्मननम्
blocks.directed: [slowly] सुखदुःखयोर्बहिर्मननम्

blocks.text: Sukhaduḥkhayor bahirmananam.
blocks.directed: Sukhaduḥkhayor bahirmananam.

blocks.text: Regarding pleasure and pain as external.
blocks.directed: Regarding pleasure and pain as external.

blocks.text: You’re Experiencing Pain. You Don’t Have to Become the Entire Concept of Pain.
blocks.directed: You’re Experiencing Pain. You Don’t Have to Become the Entire Concept of Pain.

blocks.text: Now, this is a genuinely subtle teaching.
blocks.directed: Now, this is a genuinely subtle teaching.

blocks.text: And one that could be very easily misunderstood.
blocks.directed: And one that could be very easily misunderstood.

blocks.text: So let’s get the Sanskrit right.
blocks.directed: So let’s get the Sanskrit right.

blocks.text: Sukha — pleasure, happiness, ease.
blocks.directed: Sukha — pleasure, happiness, ease.

blocks.text: Duḥkha — pain, suffering, distress.
blocks.directed: Duḥkha — pain, suffering, distress.

blocks.text: -yoḥ — dual genitive ending, referring to both.
blocks.directed: -yoḥ — dual genitive ending, referring to both.

blocks.text: Bahiḥ — outside, external.
blocks.directed: Bahiḥ — outside, external.

blocks.text: Mananam — considering, apprehending, reflecting.
blocks.directed: Mananam — considering, apprehending, reflecting.

blocks.text: So:
blocks.directed: [short pause] So:

blocks.text: The yogi apprehends pleasure and pain as something external to their true conscious identity.
blocks.directed: The yogi apprehends pleasure and pain as something external to their true conscious identity.

blocks.text: Now hang on.
blocks.directed: Now hang on.

blocks.text: Surely pain is experienced internally?
blocks.directed: Surely pain is experienced internally?

blocks.text: If you have a headache, you don’t ordinarily experience it as occurring inside a distant mountain.
blocks.directed: If you have a headache, you don’t ordinarily experience it as occurring inside a distant mountain.

blocks.text: It’s happening here.
blocks.directed: It’s happening here.

blocks.text: And if you’re happy, that happiness is part of your lived experience.
blocks.directed: And if you’re happy, that happiness is part of your lived experience.

blocks.text: So what on earth does Kṣemarāja mean by external?
blocks.directed: So what on earth does Kṣemarāja mean by external?

blocks.text: He doesn’t mean pleasure and pain are physically located outside the body.
blocks.directed: He doesn’t mean pleasure and pain are physically located outside the body.

blocks.text: He’s making a distinction between:
blocks.directed: [short pause] He’s making a distinction between:

blocks.text: Aham — the fundamental I-consciousness.
blocks.directed: Aham — the fundamental I-consciousness.

blocks.text: And:
blocks.directed: [short pause] And:

blocks.text: Idam — the realm of appearing objects and experiences.
blocks.directed: Idam — the realm of appearing objects and experiences.

blocks.text: In ordinary life, we don’t merely experience pleasure or pain.
blocks.directed: In ordinary life, we don’t merely experience pleasure or pain.

blocks.text: We identify with them.
blocks.directed: We identify with them.

blocks.text: “I am happy.”
blocks.directed: [short pause] “I am happy.”

blocks.text: “I am miserable.”
blocks.directed: [short pause] “I am miserable.”

blocks.text: “I am suffering.”
blocks.directed: [short pause] “I am suffering.”

blocks.text: And those statements can become deeply entangled with our sense of identity.
blocks.directed: And those statements can become deeply entangled with our sense of identity.

blocks.text: Now, Kṣemarāja says that the realised yogi experiences pleasure and pain differently.
blocks.directed: Now, Kṣemarāja says that the realised yogi experiences pleasure and pain differently.

blocks.text: They become apprehended as idantā — this-ness.
blocks.directed: They become apprehended as idantā — this-ness.

blocks.text: Objects or contents of experience.
blocks.directed: Objects or contents of experience.

blocks.text: Just as a blue object appears before awareness, pleasure and pain can appear without becoming the ultimate identity of the conscious subject.
blocks.directed: Just as a blue object appears before awareness, pleasure and pain can appear without becoming the ultimate identity of the conscious subject.

blocks.text: And this is a magnificent distinction.
blocks.directed: And this is a magnificent distinction.

blocks.text: Because it doesn’t require denying the experience.
blocks.directed: Because it doesn’t require denying the experience.

blocks.text: The yogi can still experience pleasure.
blocks.directed: The yogi can still experience pleasure.

blocks.text: The yogi can still experience pain.
blocks.directed: The yogi can still experience pain.

blocks.text: The body can still respond.
blocks.directed: The body can still respond.

blocks.text: The mind can still register changing conditions.
blocks.directed: The mind can still register changing conditions.

blocks.text: But the fundamental identity is no longer exhausted by them.
blocks.directed: But the fundamental identity is no longer exhausted by them.

blocks.text: And Kṣemarāja explicitly explains that pleasure and pain arise through contact with objects.
blocks.directed: And Kṣemarāja explicitly explains that pleasure and pain arise through contact with objects.

blocks.text: The realised yogi apprehends them as appearances within consciousness, rather than through the ordinary limited identification that makes them seem to define the Self.
blocks.directed: The realised yogi apprehends them as appearances within consciousness, rather than through the ordinary limited identification that makes them seem to define the Self.

blocks.text: Now, a very important qualification.
blocks.directed: Now, a very important qualification.

blocks.text: This does not mean that pain is imaginary, that bodily suffering should be ignored, or that the spiritual ideal is emotional numbness.
blocks.directed: This does not mean that pain is imaginary, that bodily suffering should be ignored, or that the spiritual ideal is emotional numbness.

blocks.text: Nor is it evidence that advanced practitioners cannot experience physical pain.
blocks.directed: Nor is it evidence that advanced practitioners cannot experience physical pain.

blocks.text: The traditional claim concerns the metaphysical identity of the experiencer, not the abolition of ordinary human physiology.
blocks.directed: The traditional claim concerns the metaphysical identity of the experiencer, not the abolition of ordinary human physiology.

blocks.text: And Kṣemarāja is very precise about this.
blocks.directed: And Kṣemarāja is very precise about this.

blocks.text: He says that the yogi has transcended identification with puryaṣṭaka as the ultimate knower.
blocks.directed: He says that the yogi has transcended identification with puryaṣṭaka as the ultimate knower.

blocks.text: Remember puryaṣṭaka?
blocks.directed: Remember puryaṣṭaka?

blocks.text: The eightfold subtle constitution.
blocks.directed: The eightfold subtle constitution.

blocks.text: Buddhi.
blocks.directed: Buddhi.

blocks.text: Ahaṃkāra.
blocks.directed: [slowly] Ahaṃkāra.

blocks.text: Manas.
blocks.directed: Manas.

blocks.text: And the five subtle sensory elements.
blocks.directed: And the five subtle sensory elements.

blocks.text: Ordinarily, the individual identifies with this mental and subtle apparatus.
blocks.directed: Ordinarily, the individual identifies with this mental and subtle apparatus.

blocks.text: And therefore the pleasure and pain occurring through it become appropriated as the defining experiences of the self.
blocks.directed: And therefore the pleasure and pain occurring through it become appropriated as the defining experiences of the self.

blocks.text: But once that identification is overcome, pleasure and pain no longer have the same power to define the ultimate subject.
blocks.directed: But once that identification is overcome, pleasure and pain no longer have the same power to define the ultimate subject.

blocks.text: Kṣemarāja cites the Īśvarapratyabhijñāvimarśinī and the Spandakārikā to make the distinction between the supreme experiencer and changing pleasure-pain cognitions. Sanskrit & Trika Shaivism.
blocks.directed: Kṣemarāja cites the Īśvarapratyabhijñāvimarśinī and the Spandakārikā to make the distinction between the supreme experiencer and changing pleasure-pain cognitions. Sanskrit & Trika Shaivism.

blocks.text: Now consider a practical analogy.
blocks.directed: Now consider a practical analogy.

blocks.text: You’re sitting quietly.
blocks.directed: You’re sitting quietly.

blocks.text: A difficult emotion arises.
blocks.directed: A difficult emotion arises.

blocks.text: Perhaps sadness.
blocks.directed: Perhaps sadness.

blocks.text: The ordinary mental structure might immediately become:
blocks.directed: [short pause] The ordinary mental structure might immediately become:

blocks.text: “I am sad.”
blocks.directed: [short pause] “I am sad.”

blocks.text: Then:
blocks.directed: [short pause] Then:

blocks.text: “My life is sad.”
blocks.directed: [short pause] “My life is sad.”

blocks.text: Then:
blocks.directed: [short pause] Then:

blocks.text: “I have always been sad.”
blocks.directed: [short pause] “I have always been sad.”

blocks.text: Then:
blocks.directed: [short pause] Then:

blocks.text: “I will always be sad.”
blocks.directed: [short pause] “I will always be sad.”

blocks.text: And within a few moments, a passing emotional condition has developed into an entire autobiography.
blocks.directed: And within a few moments, a passing emotional condition has developed into an entire autobiography.

blocks.text: You’ve gone from one feeling to a forty-seven-volume historical account of your own misery.
blocks.directed: You’ve gone from one feeling to a forty-seven-volume historical account of your own misery.

blocks.text: Very impressive.
blocks.directed: Very impressive.

blocks.text: But suppose the emotion is recognised as an appearance within awareness.
blocks.directed: But suppose the emotion is recognised as an appearance within awareness.

blocks.text: The sadness remains.
blocks.directed: The sadness remains.

blocks.text: It doesn’t have to be suppressed.
blocks.directed: It doesn’t have to be suppressed.

blocks.text: But the total identification with it can loosen.
blocks.directed: But the total identification with it can loosen.

blocks.text: There’s sadness.
blocks.directed: There’s sadness.

blocks.text: There’s awareness of sadness.
blocks.directed: There’s awareness of sadness.

blocks.text: And the whole experience is not necessarily reducible to the statement:
blocks.directed: [short pause] And the whole experience is not necessarily reducible to the statement:

blocks.text: “This is the entirety of what I am.”
blocks.directed: [short pause] “This is the entirety of what I am.”

blocks.text: Now, that is a contemporary contemplative analogy, not a complete description of Kṣemarāja’s nondual realisation.
blocks.directed: Now, that is a contemporary contemplative analogy, not a complete description of Kṣemarāja’s nondual realisation.

blocks.text: His claim is far more metaphysical.
blocks.directed: His claim is far more metaphysical.

blocks.text: But it illustrates the shift from identification with a changing experience to recognition of the conscious reality through which it appears.
blocks.directed: But it illustrates the shift from identification with a changing experience to recognition of the conscious reality through which it appears.

blocks.text: And here’s something important.
blocks.directed: And here’s something important.

blocks.text: The purpose isn’t to construct a permanently detached observer who sits coldly behind experience.
blocks.directed: The purpose isn’t to construct a permanently detached observer who sits coldly behind experience.

blocks.text: That would risk turning the Self into another subtle individual subject, separate from the objects it witnesses.
blocks.directed: That would risk turning the Self into another subtle individual subject, separate from the objects it witnesses.

blocks.text: In Trika, the supreme consciousness is inseparable from Śakti.
blocks.directed: In Trika, the supreme consciousness is inseparable from Śakti.

blocks.text: It is the source of the entire manifest field.
blocks.directed: It is the source of the entire manifest field.

blocks.text: Therefore the recognition is not ultimately a division between a pure observer and an impure world.
blocks.directed: Therefore the recognition is not ultimately a division between a pure observer and an impure world.

blocks.text: It’s the recognition that pleasure and pain are manifest within consciousness without exhausting its nature.
blocks.directed: It’s the recognition that pleasure and pain are manifest within consciousness without exhausting its nature.

blocks.text: And now comes the extraordinary implication.
blocks.directed: And now comes the extraordinary implication.

blocks.text: If the yogi is no longer inwardly bound by pleasure and pain, what condition have they attained?
blocks.directed: If the yogi is no longer inwardly bound by pleasure and pain, what condition have they attained?

blocks.text: Vasugupta has a word.
blocks.directed: Vasugupta has a word.

blocks.text: Kevalī.
blocks.directed: [slowly] Kevalī.

blocks.text: The one who stands in the purity of their own conscious nature.
blocks.directed: The one who stands in the purity of their own conscious nature.

blocks.text: And that’s where we’re going next.
blocks.directed: And that’s where we’re going next.
